stem: Which nursing focus is most consistent with end-of-life comfort care for a dying client?

options.A: Limit direct care and interaction to avoid all stimulation.
options.B: Set aside the client's expressed wishes whenever the care team prefers a different plan.
options.C: Continue burdensome curative treatment regardless of the client's goals.
options.D: Relieve pain and other distressing symptoms while supporting emotional, spiritual, practical, and family needs according to the client's wishes.

rationale: The NIH National Institute on Aging describes end-of-life care as addressing physical comfort, mental and emotional needs, spiritual needs, and practical concerns, while supporting family and following the person's end-of-life wishes. D is correct.
educational_objective: Prioritize multidimensional comfort and the client's goals during end-of-life care.
source_document_title: Providing Care and Comfort at the End of Life
source_version_date: Content reviewed November 17, 2022; current NIH page checked 2026-08-17
source_locator: What is end-of-life care?; physical comfort; mental and emotional needs; spiritual needs; family support
source_claim_supported: End-of-life care should follow the person's wishes and address physical comfort, emotional/mental needs, spiritual needs, practical concerns, and support for family.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort — end-of-life care, symptom relief, and comfort measures
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — end-of-life comfort care

source_original.stem: A nurse is providing end-of-life comfort care for a dying client. Priority comfort measures generally include:

options.A: Limiting most forms of direct care and interaction, in the belief that this reduces unnecessary stimulation
options.B: Setting aside the client's and family's expressed wishes in favor of the care team's own clinical priorities
options.C: Continuing aggressive curative treatment measures despite the client's stated preference to focus on comfort
options.D: Effective pain and symptom management, along with attention to psychological, spiritual, and family support needs

source_original.rationale: End-of-life comfort (palliative) care prioritizes effective pain and symptom management (such as addressing dyspnea, nausea, or anxiety), along with attention to the psychological, spiritual, and emotional needs of both the client and family, focusing on dignity and quality of remaining life rather than curative intervention, in alignment with the client's and family's wishes.
source_original.source_detail: End-of-life palliative care: symptom relief plus psychosocial, spiritual, and family support; reviewed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Replaced the nonspecific NHPCO homepage with an NIH/NIA end-of-life care page that explicitly covers physical, emotional, spiritual, practical, family, and preference-based care; corrected wording so family wishes do not override a capable client's own wishes.

audit_findings.currentness: NIH page remains current and was checked 2026-08-17.
audit_findings.claim_audit: All multidimensional comfort domains and respect for the person's wishes are directly supported.

distractor_audit.A: Comfort care still includes active supportive care.
distractor_audit.C: Contradicts a comfort-focused goal when the client chooses it.

audit_findings.blueprint: End-of-life comfort fits Basic Care and Comfort.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked NIH comfort domains and preference language; D remains unique.
